mainTopic: Returning stolen, borrowed and deposited items: where to return them, doubts about owing, and quietly returning a stolen lamb
overview: The amud opens with the last line of the earlier discussion about a stolen field. A cow lying on the field is swept away by a river, and רבי אלעזר and the רבנן each rule by their own known view. Then a משנה teaches that a robber, borrower or שומר who received something in a settled area may not give it back in the wilderness, unless that was agreed at the start. אביי settles a contradiction from a ברייתא: a lender may demand his loan anywhere, but a borrower cannot force repayment in the wilderness. A second משנה rules that someone who is unsure whether he paid back must pay, but someone unsure whether he ever owed is exempt. The גמרא brings the famous argument over 'You owe me a מנה' met by 'I don't know': ברי ושמא ברי עדיף against leaving money with its holder. A third משנה deals with a thief who quietly returns a stolen lamb. רב, שמואל, רבי יוחנן and רב חסדא each read differently when the owners' count of the flock frees him. The amud ends as רבא begins to speak, and his words continue on the next amud.

steps.title: The cow in the stolen field: each side stays consistent
steps.stepSummary: The previous discussion ends by describing a case: a cow lying in a stolen field is swept away by a river. רבי אלעזר and the רבנן each rule according to their own known views.
steps.simpleTranslation: A cow was lying in the field, and a river swept it away. רבי אלעזר follows his own reasoning, and the רבנן follow theirs.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of the earlier discussion about a stolen field. It names a case where the dispute between רבי אלעזר and the רבנן makes a real difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר holds that a robber does acquire land the way he acquires other stolen things. So the robber also takes on the cow lying on it, and he must pay when the river carries it off. The רבנן hold that land cannot be stolen in that way, so the robber never took on the land or the cow.

keyTerms.meaning: Lying down, crouching (said of an animal)

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new topic. It is the end of the previous סוגיא about stealing land. The new topic only starts with the משנה in the next step.

phrases.english: A cow lying in it,
phrases.notes: "In it" means in the stolen field from the earlier discussion.

phrases.english: and a river swept it away;
Rabbi Elazar follows his own reasoning,
and the Rabbis follow their own reasoning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the previous discussion of stolen land, which started before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case where they argue is a cow lying in the stolen field that a river swept away. Each side follows his own view about whether land can be acquired by a robber.

steps.title: משנה: no returning in the wilderness what was received in a settled area
steps.stepSummary: Something stolen, borrowed, or deposited in a settled area may not be given back in the wilderness. If the two sides agreed from the start to return it in the wilderness, he may.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone robs another person, borrows from him, or receives a deposit from him in a settled area, he may not give it back to him in the wilderness. If it was given on condition that he may go out and return it in the wilderness, he may return it in the wilderness.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on where a robber, borrower, or שומר must give back what he owes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the wilderness the owner gets little use from the item and has a hard time guarding it. So the one who owes cannot force it on him there. A clear agreement made at the start overrides this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit left with a שומר

steps.whatToRemember: Basic rule: what you received in a settled area, you give back in a settled area. Only an agreement made at the start allows returning it in the wilderness.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who robs his fellow
or who borrowed from him
or with whom he deposited something,
in a settled area –
he may not return it to him in the wilderness.
If it was on condition to go out to the wilderness –
he may return it to him in the wilderness.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַגּוֹזֵל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ אוֹ שֶׁהִלְוָה הֵימֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the stolen field discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Something received in a settled area may not be returned in the wilderness unless that was agreed from the start.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to say a loan can be repaid anywhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא saying a loan is repaid in any place. That seems to contradict the משנה, which forbids repaying in the wilderness.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא raises a contradiction: a loan is repaid in any place, but a lost item and a deposit are returned only in their own place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה with a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite about loans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה put a borrower in the same group as a robber and a שומר: none of them may give back in the wilderness. The ברייתא splits them up. It says a loan works anywhere, and only a lost item and a deposit are tied to their place. So for loans, the two sources seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: And they contrasted it, meaning here is a contradicting source
In their place, the same kind of place where they were received

phrases.english: GEMARA:
And they raised a contradiction:
A loan is repaid in any place,
a lost item and a deposit
are returned only in their place!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's rule about loans.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a borrower may not repay in the wilderness.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says a loan is repaid in any place, which would include the wilderness.

steps.title: אביי: the ברייתא is about the lender demanding, not the borrower paying
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the ברייתא means the lender may demand his loan anywhere. A lost item or a deposit may only be demanded in its own place. The משנה, by contrast, is about the borrower trying to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: this is what the ברייתא means. A loan may be demanded in any place. A lost item and a deposit may be demanded only in their own place.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction by explaining the ברייתא differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is talking about the lender's right to demand payment, and he can do that even in the wilderness. The משנה is talking about the borrower's right to push payment on the lender, and in the wilderness the lender may refuse. So the two sources deal with different people acting, and there is no clash.
steps.whatToRemember: A lender can demand anywhere, but a borrower cannot force repayment in the wilderness. A deposit or lost item can be demanded only in its own place.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read מִשְׁתַּלֶּמֶת as "the borrower may pay anywhere." אביי reads it as "the lender may demand anywhere."

phrases.english: Abaye said: This is what it is saying:
A loan may be claimed in any place,
a lost item and a deposit may not be claimed
except in their place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the ברייתא as being about the owner's claim, not about repayment by the one who owes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא lets the borrower repay anywhere, against the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lender may demand anywhere, but the borrower may not force repayment in the wilderness.

steps.title: Why teach that a condition works? Isn't it obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ending about a condition to return in the wilderness and asks why this needs saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: "On condition to go out to the wilderness." That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's last clause and asks why it is needed. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both sides openly agreed to return the item in the wilderness, of course the agreement holds. So the clause seems to teach nothing new.

phrases.english: "On condition to go out to the wilderness."
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting the end of the משנה.

phrases.english: That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to analyze the last clause of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's clause allowing return in the wilderness when there was a condition.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An open agreement is plainly binding, so the clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The case: the condition came up only as a passing remark
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a case where the owner mentions he is going to the wilderness, and the שומר replies that he is going there too and will return it there if needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case like this. The owner told him, "Let this deposit be with you, because I am going out to the wilderness." The שומר answered, "I also need to go out to the wilderness. If I need to return it to you, I will return it to you there."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה is speaking about a less obvious case, where the "condition" came up only in casual conversation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody here said the formal words "on condition." The owner only mentioned his trip, and the שומר added his own plan. The חידוש is that this exchange still counts as an agreement, so the שומר may return the deposit in the wilderness.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for a special case)

steps.whatToRemember: An agreement to return something in the wilderness works even if it came up only in casual conversation like this, without formal "on condition" wording.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary,
where he said to him:
phrases.notes: The owner of the deposit is speaking to the שומר.

phrases.english: "Let this deposit be with you,
since I am going out to the wilderness,"
and he said to him:
"I also need to go out to the wilderness.
If I need to return them to you,
there I will return them to you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the "obvious" question from step 5 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Setting up a specific case where the condition was not stated formally.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a formally stated condition would allow returning the deposit in the wilderness.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a passing exchange like this one counts as an agreement allowing return in the wilderness.

steps.title: New משנה: unsure if he paid versus unsure if he ever owed
steps.stepSummary: If someone admits he robbed, borrowed, or received a deposit but doesn't know if he returned it, he must pay. If he doesn't know whether there was ever a robbery, loan, or deposit, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person tells his friend: 'I robbed you,' or 'You lent me money,' or 'You gave me something to watch, and I don't know if I gave it back,' he must pay. But if he says: 'I don't know if I robbed you,' or 'if you lent me,' or 'if you gave me something to watch,' he does not have to pay.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives two cases of a person who is unsure, and the two cases get opposite rulings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case the debt is known for sure, and only the repayment is in doubt, so he must pay. In the second case it is not even known that a debt ever existed, so he is exempt. The משנה does not say here whether the other person is actively claiming the money. The גמרא asks about that in Step 10 and answers it in Step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: Must pay / does not have to pay

steps.confusionAlert: Both cases sound like 'I don't know,' but the doubt is about different things. In the first case he is unsure about paying back. In the second he is unsure about ever owing at all.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who says to his fellow: 'I robbed you';
'You lent me'; 'You deposited something with me,
and I do not know if I returned it to you

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא הֶחְזַרְתִּי לָךְ״ – חַיָּיב לְשַׁלֵּם.
phrases.english: or if I did not return it to you' – he is liable to pay.
But if he said to him:
'I do not know if I robbed you';
'if you lent me'; 'if you deposited something with me'
– he is exempt from paying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It moves on from the topic of returning items in the wilderness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the debt is certain but repayment is in doubt, he must pay. If the debt itself is in doubt, he is exempt.

steps.title: The dispute over 'You owe me a מנה' and 'I don't know'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a מחלוקת. When the claimant is sure and the defendant says 'I don't know,' רב הונא and רב יהודה say he must pay, and רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן say he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was said: One person says, 'I have a מנה in your hands,' and the other says, 'I don't know.' רב הונא and רב יהודה say he must pay. רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן say he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related argument between אמוראים about a sure claim met by an unsure answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the claimant is certain, and the defendant honestly does not know. The question is whether the claimant's certainty is enough to take money from the defendant, who is unsure.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was stated:
'I have a maneh in your hand,'
phrases.notes: He means: you owe me a מנה, which is 100 דינרים.

phrases.english: and the other says: 'I do not know'

phrases.aramaic: – רַב הוּנָא וְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמְרִי: חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: – Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say: he is liable,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב נַחְמָן וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמְרִי: פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yoḥanan say: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a מחלוקת about the same kind of doubt that the משנה discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא and רב יהודה say he is liable. רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן say he is exempt.

steps.title: The reasons on each side
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא and רב יהודה say a sure claim beats an unsure one (ברי ושמא ברי עדיף). רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן say money stays with whoever holds it now.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא and רב יהודה say he must pay, because when one side is sure and the other is unsure, the sure side wins. רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן say he is exempt, because we leave the money with its owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind each opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side looks at the strength of the claims: a sure claim is stronger than 'I don't know.' The other side looks at who holds the money now. You cannot take money away from someone without clear proof, and a claim alone is not proof.

keyTerms.meaning: When one side is certain and the other is unsure, the certain side wins
Leave the money with its present owner
The current status; who holds the money now

steps.whatToRemember: ברי ושמא ברי עדיף (the sure claim wins) is the reasoning of רב הונא and רב יהודה. אוקי ממונא בחזקת מריה (money stays where it is) is the reasoning of רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן.
steps.whyThisMatters: These two principles come up again and again across ש״ס whenever a sure claim meets an unsure answer.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא וְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמְרִי חַיָּיב –
phrases.english: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say he is liable –
a certain claim against an uncertain one, the certain one is stronger.

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמְרִי פָּטוּר –
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yoḥanan say he is exempt –
leave the money in the possession of its owner.
phrases.notes: The 'owner' here is the person holding the money now, the one who says 'I don't know.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasons behind the two opinions just stated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liable because the sure claim wins. Exempt because money stays with its holder.

steps.title: The end of the משנה challenges רב הונא and רב יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה exempts someone who says 'I don't know if you lent me.' This must be a case where the lender is actively claiming, which goes against רב הונא and רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if he says 'I don't know if you lent me,' he is exempt. What is the case? If the lender is not claiming the money, then the first part of the משנה is also about a case with no claim, so why would he have to pay there? So it must be that the lender is claiming, and still the end of the משנה says he is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the end of the משנה to attack the opinion of רב הונא and רב יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא argues that both halves of the משנה must describe the same setting. The first half says 'must pay,' which only makes sense if the lender is claiming. So the second half is also a case where the lender claims for sure, and the borrower is still exempt. That fits רב נחמן and רבי יוחנן and goes against 'the sure claim wins.'

keyTerms.meaning: The first part / the last part of a משנה

phrases.english: We learned: But if he said to him:
'I do not know if you lent me' – he is exempt.
What are the circumstances?
If you say that the lender is not claiming from him –

phrases.aramaic: רֵישָׁא נָמֵי דְּלָא קָא תָבַע לֵיהּ;
phrases.english: then the first clause is also where he is not claiming from him;
phrases.notes: The first clause is 'You lent me, and I don't know if I paid you back.'

phrases.english: why is he liable?
Rather, it is where he is claiming from him,
and the latter clause teaches: he is exempt from paying!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the מחלוקת against the משנה from step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא and רב יהודה (the sure claim wins)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both halves of the משנה must involve an active claim. In the second half the lender claims for sure, and the borrower who says 'I don't know' is still exempt. That goes against 'the sure claim wins.'

steps.title: The משנה's exempt case is where the lender is not claiming
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רב הונא and רב יהודה. The exempt case in the משנה is where the lender makes no claim at all, and the first clause's 'liable' means only an obligation to Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really, the משנה is talking about a case where the lender is not claiming anything from him. And the first clause, where he must pay, is about someone who wants to fulfill his duty to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the קשיא from Step 10 by saying the משנה's 'I don't know if you lent me' case has no claimant at all. So it does not contradict רב הונא and רב יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא and רב יהודה only say 'pay' when the other side is sure and actively claiming (ברי ושמא). If nobody is claiming, there is no sure claim to win, so the exemption fits their view. The first clause ('I don't know if I returned it, so pay') then must be about a duty to Heaven, not something a בית דין forces, since there is no claimant there either.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually — introduces the true reading of the case
The first clause of the משנה
To fulfill one's duty to Heaven, beyond what a court can force

steps.confusionAlert: 'Liable' in the first clause here does not mean a בית דין will make him pay. It means that if he wants to be honest before Heaven, he should pay.

phrases.aramaic: לָא; לְעוֹלָם דְּלָא קָא תָבַע לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: No; really, it is where he is not claiming from him,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the lender. He isn't demanding anything, so there is no sure claim against the borrower.

phrases.english: and the first clause is where he comes to fulfill his duty to Heaven.
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case from Step 7: 'I don't know if I returned it' — pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; לְעוֹלָם דְּלָא קָא תָבַע לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the קשיא of Step 10 by redefining the משנה's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case (אוקימתא): there is no claimant, and the 'liable' clause is only a heavenly duty.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's exemption for 'I don't know if you lent me' is about a case where the lender is claiming. That would go against רב הונא and רב יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה has no claimant. So ברי ושמא never comes up, and רב הונא and רב יהודה stand.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן also speaks of being liable 'to fulfill duty to Heaven'
steps.stepSummary: A statement of רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יוחנן is brought. It uses the same idea of being liable only to fulfill one's duty to Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: if someone says to another, 'I have a מנה in your hand,' and the other says, 'I don't know,' he is liable — when he wants to fulfill his duty to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the idea it just used. There is a kind of 'liable' that means only a duty to Heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן holds that a court does not force the 'I don't know' defendant to pay (Step 8). Even so, he says that before Heaven the defendant should pay. This shows the category 'liable to fulfill one's duty to Heaven' is a real, accepted idea, just as the תירוץ used it.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated — brings a supporting teaching
A sum of one hundred דינרים

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
One who says to his fellow: 'I have a maneh in your hand,'
and the other says: 'I don't know' — he is liable,
where he comes to fulfill his duty to Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי, אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the concept used in the תירוץ of Step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That 'liable' can mean only an obligation to fulfill one's duty to Heaven.
steps.raayaSupportSource: An אמורא statement of רבי יוחנן, reported by רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.whatToRemember: When the claimant is sure and the defendant says 'I don't know,' רבי יוחנן says a court cannot force payment. But the defendant should pay to fulfill his duty to Heaven.

steps.title: New משנה: a lamb stolen and quietly returned
steps.stepSummary: A thief returns a stolen lamb without telling anyone. He stays responsible if it later dies or is stolen. But if the owners never knew of the theft or return, and counted the flock and found it complete, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone stole a lamb from the flock and returned it, and then it died or was stolen. He is responsible for it. If the owners knew neither about the theft nor about the return, and they counted the sheep and the flock was complete, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins, about when a thief's quiet return of a stolen animal counts as a real return.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just putting the lamb back is not enough. The thief stays responsible, as if he still had it. But in the second case the owners never knew anything happened. There, the owners' count of a complete flock ends his responsibility.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who steals a lamb from the flock and returns it,
and it died or was stolen — he is responsible for it.
If the owners did not know
neither about its theft nor about its return,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָנוּ אֶת הַצֹּאן וּשְׁלֵימָה הִיא – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and they counted the sheep and it was complete — he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַגּוֹנֵב טָלֶה מִן הָעֵדֶר וְהֶחְזִירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic; not connected to the ברי ושמא discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quietly returning a stolen lamb does not end the thief's responsibility. But if the owners never knew of the theft, counted the flock and found it whole, he is exempt.

steps.title: רב: if the owners knew of the theft, they must know of the return
steps.stepSummary: רב explains the משנה. If the owners knew of the theft, the return must also be with their knowledge. If they did not know, a count of the flock is enough. The counting clause refers only to the second case.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב said: When it was with their knowledge, the return needs their knowledge. When it was without their knowledge, a count exempts him. And when the משנה teaches 'they counted the sheep and it was complete,' that is about the second clause.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains how to read the two cases of the משנה. He says when a count is enough and when the owners must actually know about the return.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owners knew their lamb was stolen, they stop watching it as part of the flock. So only telling them about the return puts it back under their care. If they never knew, they kept watching the whole flock all along, and a complete count shows it is back in their care. That is why רב says the counting line belongs only to the סיפא.

keyTerms.meaning: With knowledge — the owners knew of the theft
Needs knowledge — the owners must know of the return
The last clause of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'they counted and it was whole' as working for both cases. רב says a count helps only when the owners never knew about the theft.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: if the owners knew of the theft, the thief must make sure they know of the return. If they never knew, their counting the flock and finding it complete is enough.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav said:
With knowledge — it requires knowledge.
phrases.notes: If the owners knew about the theft, they must also know about the return.

phrases.english: Without knowledge — a count exempts.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי קָתָנֵי ״וּמָנוּ אֶת הַצֹּאן וְהִיא שְׁלֵימָה״ – אַסֵּיפָא.
phrases.english: And when it teaches 'and they counted the sheep and it was complete' — that refers to the last clause.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how to read the משנה just quoted in Step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the owners knew of the theft, the return must be with their knowledge. If they did not know, a count of the flock exempts the thief.

steps.title: שמואל: Counting Works Whether or Not the Owners Knew
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that the owners' count of the flock frees the thief in every case. So the counting clause in the משנה applies to the whole משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל says: whether the owners knew about the theft or did not know, their counting the flock frees the thief. When the משנה says 'they counted and it was whole, he is exempt,' that goes on the whole משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives his own reading of the משנה, which differs from רב's. For him, counting the flock is enough to free the thief, whether or not the owners knew about the theft.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said counting helps only when the owners never knew about the theft. If they knew, the return had to be done with their knowledge. שמואל disagrees: counting works even when they knew, so the counting line covers both cases in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: With knowledge: here, the owners knew about the theft
Without knowledge: the owners never knew about the theft
On all of it: applies to the whole משנה

phrases.english: And Shmuel says:
Whether with knowledge or without knowledge,
phrases.notes: The 'knowledge' here is the owners' knowledge of the theft.

phrases.english: counting exempts him,
and when it teaches: 'And they counted and it was whole, he is exempt,'
it refers to all of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: בֵּין לְדַעַת בֵּין שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב's reading in step 14 and gives a broader role to counting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Counting the flock frees the thief whether or not the owners knew of the theft. The counting clause goes on the whole משנה.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: If the Owners Never Knew, Not Even Counting Is Needed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says counting frees the thief when the owners knew about the theft. When they did not know, nothing at all is needed. The counting clause goes only on the first case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: if the owners knew about the theft, their counting frees the thief. If they did not know, even counting is not needed. When the משנה says 'they counted the flock and it was whole,' that goes on the first case.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a third reading of the משנה. When the owners knew, counting is enough. When they never knew, the thief is free just by putting the lamb back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of רב. רב said counting helps only when the owners did not know. רבי יוחנן says counting is for when they did know. When they never knew, he needs nothing at all, so the counting line belongs only to the first case.

keyTerms.meaning: On the first clause: applies only to the opening case of the משנה
The first part of a משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רב and רבי יוחנן: they are mirror images. רב puts counting on the 'did not know' case. רבי יוחנן puts it on the 'knew' case and requires nothing when the owners did not know.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan says:
With knowledge, counting exempts him;

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת – אֲפִילּוּ מִנְיָן נָמֵי לָא צְרִיךְ.
phrases.english: without knowledge, even counting is also not needed.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי קָתָנֵי: ״וּמָנוּ אֶת הַצֹּאן וְהִיא שְׁלֵימָה״ –
phrases.english: And when it teaches: 'And they counted the flock and it was whole,'
it refers to the first clause.
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case where the owners knew about the theft.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אוֹמֵר: לְדַעַת מִנְיָן פּוֹטֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further alternative reading after רב and שמואל. It is the most lenient when the owners did not know.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the owners knew, counting frees the thief. If they did not know, nothing is required. The counting clause applies to the first case only.

steps.title: רב חסדא: If the Owners Never Knew, They Must Be Told
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא agrees that counting frees the thief when the owners knew. When they did not know, the return must be done with their knowledge. The counting clause goes on the first case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא says: if the owners knew about the theft, their counting frees the thief. If they did not know, the return needs their knowledge. When the משנה says 'they counted the flock and it was whole,' that goes on the first case.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a fourth reading of the משנה. He agrees with רבי יוחנן about the 'knew' case. But he is strict in the 'did not know' case: counting is not enough, and the owners must be made aware.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא and רבי יוחנן agree on two points: counting works when the owners knew, and the counting line goes on the first case. They split on the 'did not know' case. רבי יוחנן needs nothing, while רב חסדא needs the owners' knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: Requires knowledge: the owners must be aware of the return

steps.whatToRemember: There are four views on this משנה. רב: knew means a return with knowledge; did not know means counting. שמואל: counting works in both cases. רבי יוחנן: knew means counting; did not know means nothing needed. רב חסדא: knew means counting; did not know means knowledge needed.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב חסדא's view looks surprising: the owners who never knew need more than the ones who knew. That is likely why the גמרא now turns to רבא.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda says:
With knowledge, counting exempts him;
without knowledge, knowledge is required.
phrases.notes: He means the lamb must be returned with the owners knowing about it.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי קָתָנֵי: ״וּמָנוּ אֶת הַצֹּאן וְהִיא שְׁלֵימָה״ –
phrases.english: And when it teaches: 'And they counted the flock and it was whole,'
it refers to the first clause.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: לְדַעַת מִנְיָן פּוֹטֵר, שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעַת צָרִיךְ דַּעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shares רבי יוחנן's handling of the first case but is strict where רבי יוחנן was lenient.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the owners knew, counting frees the thief. If they did not know, the return must be made with their knowledge. The counting clause applies to the first case only.

steps.deeperAnalysis: After four different readings of the משנה, רבא now steps in. His words begin on the next amud, and there we will see how they connect to the views above.
